title: kube-proxy should periodically resync iptables to recover from unexpected drift
body:
### What would you like to be added?

kube-proxy performs a periodic full resync of iptables to correct unexpected drift between expected and actual iptables state.

### Why is this needed?

Today, kube-proxy performs a full resync of iptables only under certain conditions. In AKS, we have sometimes seen cases where iptables rules are accidentally modified (e.g. by daemonsets installed by a customer). Without some trigger (like a restart or endpoints created/deleted), kube-proxy won't detect or correct the drift between the actual/expected state of iptables.

A specific scenario in which this can happen:
1. iptables monitor polls until the canary chain in the mangle table is flushed, but doesn't check the canary chains in NAT or filter table: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d001d5684e69b08e120dc328917925318c5f324c/pkg/util/iptables/iptables.go#L586

title: support set default dns ndots in kubelet
body:
# What would you like to be added?
support set default dns ndots in kubelet
such as --dns-default-ndtos=2

# Why is this needed?
For ultra-large-scale clusters, there are hundreds of thousands of nodes and millions of pods. At the same time, a centralized DNS architecture is adopted. All DNS requests will be sent to the central DNS service cluster. At this time, each pod will be resolved once more or less, which will have a great impact on the pressure of the DNS server. The ndots configuration can determine whether to resolve the original domain name first and then splice it, or to splice it first and then resolve it, which will effectively affect the number of DNS resolutions for each pod. For this scenario, we prefer a unified default configuration instead of requiring users to configure DNS ndots in the pod, so that users do not need to understand the logic here, and it will not cause greater pressure on the DNS server.

title: Add "action" property to NetworkPolicySpec

### What would you like to be added?
Add an `action` property to NetworkPolicySpec, which is an enum described as such:

* `accept` - Accept the packet
* `drop` - Drop the packet, allowing for a timeout on the other side
* `reject` - Immediately send back an error packet (such as a TCP RST)

For `iptables`, this would closely match the ACCEPT, DROP, REJECT actions, respectively.

This property could be expanded to include other actions, such as `log`, if they are compatible with the underlying sub-systems, either in the new feature, or future feature requests.
### Why is this needed?
The existing [NetworkPolicySpec](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/v1.28/#networkpolicyspec-v1-networking-k8s-io) has an implied action here described here:

> Outgoing traffic is allowed if there are no NetworkPolicies selecting the pod (and cluster policy otherwise allows the traffic), OR if the traffic matches at least one egress rule across all of the NetworkPolicy objects whose podSelector matches the pod. If this field is empty then this NetworkPolicy limits all outgoing traffic (and serves solely to ensure that the pods it selects are isolated by default).

So, the action taken for a given network policy is not explicitly declared, and could change depending on if the rules are removed or added.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

 [code] 

The docs are misleading, for example:

https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/network-policies/ 

> A pod is isolated for egress if there is any NetworkPolicy that both selects the pod and has "Egress" in its policyTypes; we say that such a policy applies to the pod for egress. When a pod is isolated for egress, **the only allowed connections from the pod are those allowed by the egress list of some NetworkPolicy that applies to the pod for egress**. The effects of those egress lists combine additively.

In truth this refers to **the only new, unestablished connections ...**.

Indeed, given https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/109672 and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/120214 it seems this design choice for TCP is not protocol-independent and an undeliberate architectural design.

title: Panic Threshold for Readiness Probe Failures
body:
### What would you like to be added?

When using external dependencies inside healthchecks or using fixed thread pool applications like python+gunicorn, ruby+passenger, PHP etc,... upstream service failures tend to cause cascading impact on the service as well.

one solution is removing the upstream services inside the healthchecks and that's how we are solving currently but that still won't solve the case where healthchecks are failing due to excessive load. like suddenly 2x requests came on service that caused some pods to reach capacity and start failing readiness probes which in turn causes a cascading impact where scheduler removes the pods from the service.

we faced similar issues in envoy and unhealthy panic threshold in envoy helped a lot - https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/upstream/load_balancing/panic_threshold

the feature has a lot of moving parts though i.e it shouldn't trigger during normal scenarios like deployments, rotating the pods of a service, interruptions in the underlying ec2 leading to replacements of pods in significant chunks.

references to similar outages - 
1. https://loft.sh/blog/kubernetes-readiness-probes-examples-and-common-pitfalls/#cascading-failures
2. https://doordash.engineering/2022/08/09/how-to-handle-kubernetes-health-checks/

### Why is this needed?

To avoid cascading outages when more than 30-40% of the pods of a deployment starts failing readiness probes

title: kube-proxy IPVS mode configured with method SourceHash and Maglev should evenly distribute connections to all endpoints
body:
### What would you like to be added?
# Problem
The current support of the load distribution method `sh` and `mh` in kube-proxy ipvs mode only performs hashing of source IP address to select endpoints. As a result, all connections from a single client (i.e. from a particular source IP) are always forwarded to only one endpoint matching with the hash value of this source IP. If the client opens a vast majority of connections to the k8s cluster, it will result in traffic imbalance as only one endpoint located on one node handles the connections while the remaining endpoints/nodes are idle. 

Here is an example of the problem when using `mh` method for kube-proxy

- Deploy a service with 4 endpoints located on 4 nodes.

 [code] 

- Open 200 connections from a client to node IP of any node (e.g. telnet 192.168.1.1 32000). All connections receive replies from only one single endpoint.

- The distribution printout also shows that all connections are forwarded to the endpoint (e.g. 1.0.4.2:5001 in this example)
 [code] 
- Similar issue is seen with `sh` method

 [code] 
### Why is this needed?
Connections from a client should be evenly distributed to all endpoints like `rr` to avoid unbalanced load distribution between cluster nodes and endpoints.

This can be easily done by enabling the source port hash flag that IPVS supports for the methods which performs hashing on both source IP and source port when selecting the target endpoint.

title: [Scheduling] Fast Host-Scoped Inter-Pod Affinity and Anti-Affinity
body:
### What would you like to be added?
The current implementation of inter-pod affinity and anti-affinity in the Kubernetes scheduler is designed for a generic case where a pod's constraints may affect any other pod in the cluster. This results in expensive global scans and map constructions during every scheduling cycle, which can lead to performance bottlenecks.
We propose to optimize the performance of a common use case: host-scoped rules where the `topologyKey` is `kubernetes.io/hostname`.
The core idea is to isolate host-scoped rules from broader topology calculations to **avoid unnecessary cluster-wide scans**.
1. **Enhanced Caching Layer**: Update the scheduler's `NodeInfo` and `NodeInfoLister` to explicitly track pods with non-host-scoped rules. This allows the scheduler to quickly identify only the specific nodes that require expensive cross-node topology calculations.
2. **Term Separation**: During the `PreFilter` phase, the plugin should split affinity and anti-affinity terms into two groups: `hostScoped` (hostname) and `nonHostScoped` (all others).
3. **Localized Filtering**: For host-scoped rules, bypass the construction of global topology maps. Instead, perform a local check against the pods on the specific node being evaluated during the `Filter` phase. This replaces global lookups with a much faster local check.

### What would you like to be added?
some slack discussion: https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0AHLJ0EAEL/p1775561714916009
Just add a few retries (with some backoff) at the pod group binding cycle's pod binding API calls. 
How many retries? -> That is a open question. 
Options in my mind:
- always the same max retries. 
- decide the max retry proportionally to the group size.

Smaller jobs later came and take over the remaining empty capacity on rack-A. The first job never lands until smaller jobs complete at the same timing, which could be nearly impossible.

body:

title: Export `validateAffinity()` as `ValidateAffinity()` for external validation consistency
body:
**Problem Statement**:
The `validateAffinity()` function in `k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/apis/core/validation` package is currently _private_ (unexported), which forces external projects that need to validate Affinity configurations to duplicate ~200 lines of validation logic.
If we need to validate Affinity, then we have to replicate the entire `validateAffinity()` logic along with its helper functions (`validateNodeAffinity`, `validatePodAffinity`, `validatePodAntiAffinity`, etc.) to pre-validate user-provided affinity configurations before deploying pods.
This duplication:
- Creates maintenance burden (keeping in sync with upstream changes)
- Risks validation drift between client-side and server-side logic
- Duplicates code that already exists and is well-tested in Kubernetes
_Similar Functions ARE already exported_:
The same package has validation methods exported for NodeSelector(`ValidateNodeSelector`), Tolerations(`ValidateTolerations`), but not for affinity.
**Proposed Solution**:
A simple, non-breaking wrapper following the existing pattern:
 [code] 
_Implementation impact_:
- Zero changes to internal logic : the private function remains unchanged
- Full backward compatibility : existing code paths unaffected
- Follows established pattern : mirrors how `ValidateTolerations` and `ValidateNodeSelector` are exported.
**Benefits**:
- Bug Discovery: External projects using server-side validation logic help identify bugs earlier. The same validation code is used by kube-apiserve

title: Support async moveAllToActiveOrBackoffQueue in scheduler
body:
### What would you like to be added?
Kube-Scheduler uses scheduling hint to determine whether the pods should be moved to ActiveQ. Scheduler will lock and traverse all pods in unschedulableQ to find which pods might become schedulable due to the incoming event. Many operation on SchedulingQueue will be blocked if the events come too frequently.
For example, if someone updates assigned pod in a high frequency, the SchedulingQueue will be blocked by assignedPodUpdate() and new pods can not be added into the activeQ, result in scheduler hang.
I want to make moveAllToActiveOrBackoffQueue run in a background goroutine, check multi cluster events once a time, and limit its frequency to avoid influencing other SchedulingQueue operation.
### Why is this needed?
If someone updates assigned pod in a high frequency, the SchedulingQueue will be blocked by assignedPodUpdate() and new pods can not be added into the activeQ, result in scheduler hang.

body:
### What would you like to be added?
With cluster events, we need to check whether we can requeue unschedulable pods into active queue or backoff queue more efficiently.
 
/assign
/cc @macsko 
### Why is this needed?
When it comes to gang scheduling, when Pod/Add event happens, it should also check unschedulable pods (because the newly added pod, along with unschedulable pods grouped together may complete the gang/workload).
Workaround was introduced is to use "MoveAllToActiveOrBackoffQueue()" inside the "Add/Pod" cluster event. But this would run queuing hints for all plugins subscribing to such event, while we are only concerned with "GangScheduling" plugin for this particular case.
### References

title: improved preemption logic for the kubernetes scheduler
body:
### What would you like to be added?
I'd like to expand the kubernetes scheduler so that multiple pods together can share the resources of a preempted pod
### Why is this needed?
According to my understanding, when a pod is preempted there can only be one pod that replaces this pod immediately (a.k.a one pod that'll get a `nominatedNode`), this can delay scheduling of other pods if a relatively big pod is preempted by a relatively small pod.
usually this wouldn't be much of a problem since other small pods will just take a bit longer to schedule, but this has risen from an [issue](https://github.com/kubernetes/autoscaler/issues/7683) in kubernetes/autoscaler, where this might cause unnecessary scale ups in cluster autoscaler.

title: Move in-tree plugins to the staging repository
body:
Continued from #89930.
 
 
/cc @kubernetes/sig-scheduling-leads @ania-borowiec 
---
We moved all interfaces, types etc from k/k to the staging repo. 
The next discussion is whether we want to move our in-tree plugins to the staging repo. 
Some external components (such as descheduler, the cluster autoscaler, Kueue etc) run the scheduling simulation today, but, for example, descheduler implements the scheduling logic on their own. 
If we can publish in-tree plugins in the staging repo and make them easier to be imported, such components may want to use in-tree plugins to run their scheduling simulation. But, we, of course, first check if this motivation is big enough before starting this initiative.
On the technical side, as summarized in [this comment of mine](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/89930#issuecomment-2566236328), plugins still have some dependencies to k/k (e.g., feature flag package). We need to think about how we remove those dependencies to make in-tree plugins able to be moved outside.

title: Support scheduling hint in Pod.Spec to have sticky scheduling
body:
### What would you like to be added?
Provide a mechanism to hint the scheduler to schedule a pod, which is to be created, to a node where the pod's owner controller believe it's optimal to schedule that specific pod to that node.
### Why is this needed?
Some batch workloads have checkpoints saved in local storage, although they can restore checkpoints from previous node's storage via network, the network overhead is non-trivial. This is common in using IndexedJob or JobSet. When there is a disruption, Pods are recreated and users have to implement mechanisms outside k8s to workaround this problem or have suboptimal performance.
Currently, `pod.status.nominatedNodeName` achieves similar logic with one drawback: the `pod.status` field can't be initialized at pod creation so pod controllers can't really rely on it otherwise race conditions may happen.

scheduler_perf: Add Memory Tracking to Detect Memory Leaks
body:
## What type of Issue is this?
 
 
## What this Issue does / why we need it:
This issue proposes adding memory tracking capabilities to `scheduler_perf` to detect memory leaks and regressions before they reach production.
### Background
The Kubernetes scheduler has experienced critical memory leaks in production:
- **#120622**: QHint inFlightPods memory leak
- **#111773**: Preemption strategy memory leak
- **#83895**: Work queue timer memory leak
- And your custom scheduler plugins?
These issues were discovered only after deployment to production, causing a significant operational impact. The variety of root causes (watch operations, preemption logic, queue timers, map cleanup) demonstrates the need for systematic memory tracking.
### Proposed Solution
Add memory tracking to `scheduler_perf` that monitors:
- **HeapMemoryInUse**: Current heap memory usage (MB)
- **GoroutineCount**: Number of active goroutines
- **MemoryGrowthRate**: Rate of memory increase (MB/min)
Frankly, what to monitor is debatable. I welcome your opinion.
PoC is https://github.com/utam0k/kubernetes/tree/scheduler-perf-memory/test/integration/scheduler_perf/memory/demo, and confirm PoC can detect #120622 case.
Here is the summary by PoC:

- **Duration**: ~1.5 minutes

title: Support for OFFLINE volume expansion using CSI driver using a rolling upgrade strategy
body:
### What would you like to be added?
Some CSI drivers (e.g. https://github.com/outscale/osc-bsu-csi-driver up to v1.7.0) support OFFLINE volume expansion only. If the users would like to resize PVC for pods controlled by StatefulSet, they should manually scale down all replicas before the external-resizer controller can resize the volumes. Otherwise, the StatefulSet controller creates the new Pod immediately without giving a chance for the _AttachDetachController_ to detach the volume from the worker.
It would be good to support OFFLINE volume expansion using the StatfulSet rolling upgrade strategy.
### Why is this needed?
Deployments with CSI drivers that support OFFLINE volume resize can still benefit from application no-downtime using a StatefulSet rolling upgrade strategy.

title: Feature Request: Support character device volumeMode in local PersistentVolumes
body:
### What would you like to be added?
Kubernetes currently supports raw block device volumes via volumeMode: Block (see [raw block volume support](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2019/03/07/raw-block-volume-support-to-beta/)). However, there is no support for raw character devices.
I would like Kubernetes to support a new `volumeMode: CharDevice` option for local volumes, allowing pods to consume character device files directly from the host (e.g., `/dev/stX` for tape drives).
### Why is this needed?
Some specialised workloads rely on hardware accessible via character devices. Without native support, these workloads cannot be containerised using standard Kubernetes volume mechanisms.
Adding support for `volumeMode: CharDevice` would enable static provisioning of local PersistentVolumes backed by character devices. This would make Kubernetes a more viable platform for tape-based systems or other software relying on character devices.

title: When updating a PV to the "Released" state, should we check whether the corresponding volume is in the attached state?
body:
### What would you like to be added?
1. After triggering the deletion of a PVC and Pod, the current logic causes the PVC-protection-controller to remove finalizers immediately upon Pod deletion, leading to the complete deletion of the PVC.
2. At this point, the VolumeAttachment might still be in the process of being detached, as the CSI driver may be calling cloud provider APIs to unbind the device, which is expected to be a time-consuming operation.
 
3. If the PV is updated to the "Released" state at this time, the external-provisioner will detect this change and attempt to perform DeleteVolume. However, the volume might still be in the attached state, causing this operation to fail and resulting in misleading error feedback.
 
### Why is this needed?
None

title: support ephemeral rw image volume mounts
body:
### What would you like to be added?
With the continued advancement of image volumes https://kubernetes.io/blog/2025/04/29/kubernetes-v1-33-image-volume-beta/ I would like to see an ability to mount the volume as rw.
I do *NOT* want the actual changes to be written to the registry (local or remote) but rather simply want the mount point to be ephemeral in much the same way a rootfs is of a running container.
### Why is this needed?
My specific use-case it to use the volume essentially as a rw cache. For example let's say I have a large git repository I wish to share across CI builds running in a cluster. I would like each build to use the image as a 'starting place' and each build will then simply (ephemerally) do a `git pull` and `git checkout` etc on the mount point and be able to generally function as a rw volume. Once the build is done the modified data is simply discarded and the source image is left untouched.
A side-benefit is that each relevant node will only store the data of the repo once (ie: copy-on-write-like semantics) reducing storage requirements. The source image can periodically be updated to the latest upstream content and inherit the goodness of image deltas for that process as well.
Thanks for the consideration!

title: Optimize volumemanager run loop
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Change how volume management tasks are scheduled to execute to reduce its overhead.

### Why is this needed?

There are two parts in volume management:

* populating the desired state of volumes
* reconciling the desired state and actual state

Both parts are scheduled to run for every [100ms](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7ec344dcef9a04920578aabe4e122bc0b3404afe/pkg/kubelet/volumemanager/volume_manager.go#L58-L62), which might be unnecessary for nodes with very steady state (e.g. standalone kubelet). 

Two optimization options:

1. Just making the run interval configurable so the users can decide accordingly. However, this not only increases the configuration complexity but also increases the latency to reconcile the volumes
2. Making the populating first watch over pod changes, which can be a signal passed from kubelet PLEG/housekeeping so populating is only triggered when there are changes in pods. Then Also making reconciling watch over signals passed by populating, which only triggers a signal when there are differences populated. This optimization could be more complicated with trivial retries to ensure the reconciliation is successfully executed.

With optimization, I expect 1%~1.5% CPU per node reduced

title: Consider deprecating or changing the default of --service-account-extend-token-expiration

### What would you like to be added?
Consider changing the default of `--service-account-extend-token-expiration` to `false` in a future release, or deprecating the flag, now that the migration it was added for is long over. If sig-auth agrees on a direction, I'm happy to pick this up, including writing a KEP or the implementation PR.
### Why is this needed?
The flag's help text says it "helps safe transition from legacy token to bound service account token feature" and that "admission injected tokens would be extended up to 1 year to prevent unexpected failure during transition" ([source](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f3a4bbacc08a3c89673419b8d3db272540160ed1/pkg/kubeapiserver/options/authentication.go#L459-L463)). Bound service account tokens went beta in 1.21, about 5 years ago. It defaults to `true`, so injected tokens are accepted for far longer than the 1 hour the pod spec implies.
Consequences of the default:
- Clients that read the token once and cache it keep working silently for the extended window and then fail all at once. With the extension off, they would fail within about an hour, where they are easy to find.
- A token that has been rotated away but leaked stays usable until the pod is deleted or the extended window ends.
- CIS Kubernetes Benchmark control 1.2.30 recommends setting it to `false`, so many distributions have to override the default to pass audits.

### What happened?
The `generateCSR()` function in `staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/certificate/certificate_manager.go` hardcodes the key type to ECDSA P-256:
 [code] 
This means all kubelet client and server certificates generated via the certificate manager use ECDSA P-256, regardless of what key type the cluster CA uses. There is no configuration option to override this.
The kubelet client certificate on the first control plane node is initially generated by `kubeadm` using the same key type as the cluster CA (typically RSA 2048), but on subsequent rotations it switches to ECDSA P-256 because rotation goes through client-go's hardcoded path.

The key type for CSR generation should be configurable via the `CertificateManager` `Config` struct, similar to how `GetUsages` is already a configurable function. For example:

1. Deploy a Kubernetes cluster with an RSA CA (default `kubeadm init` behavior).
2. Inspect the kubelet client certificate on the first control plane node — it uses RSA (same as CA).
3. Wait for certificate rotation (or force it by shortening cert lifetime).
4. After rotation, inspect the new kubelet client certificate — it is now ECDSA P-256.

## What would you like to be added?
Add a `tlsServerName` field to the `TLSConfig` structure in `EgressSelectorConfiguration` to allow overriding the hostname used for TLS certificate verification, similar to the existing `tls-server-name` field in kubeconfig (added in[ #88769](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/88769)).

This functionality already exists in:
- **kubeconfig files**: The `tls-server-name` field was added in #88769 for similar use cases

- **Go's `tls.Config`**: The underlying `ServerName` field supports this

### Use Case
This addresses scenarios where components using EgressSelectorConfiguration connect through Kubernetes Service DNS names (e.g., proxy.svc.cluster.local) but that hostname is not included in the server certificate's Subject Alternative Names (SANs), which define which hostnames a certificate is valid for.

- The proxy's TLS certificate contains SANs for: `proxy.example.com`

title: Make credential plugin policy/allowlist settable with `kubectl kuberc set`
body:
### What would you like to be added?
A new alpha command, `kubectl alpha kuberc set` has been added, which modifies the contents of the `kuberc` file. We should modify the interface to `kubectl alpha kuberc set` to make it possible to set the `credentialPluginPolicy` and `credentialPluginAllowlist` fields (added in 1.35 as an extension to KEP-3104) from the command line.
### Why is this needed?
This is needed in order to further reduce the friction for end-users in securing the `kubectl` client. `credentialPluginPolicy` and `credentialPluginAllowlist` are security knobs, and it would be great to have a simple cli one-liner to turn them on, rather than requiring the user to modify and/or create a new configuration file with which they may not be familiar. In addition, the appropriate values may depend on provider configurations, but cloud providers can likewise provide CLI one-liners to allow their plugins but no others.

title: [KMSv2] Replace DEK seed cache with non-expiring LRU cache
body:
Previously since >= 1.29, we have promoted the feature gate `KMSv2KDF` to GA and currently the KDF enablement is locked to true via:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/05a596033cbe507053d6de79b8066c7f16076080/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/encryptionconfig/config.go#L128-L130
With the KDF feature on, the cardinality of the cache for holding DEK seeds should be low and stable (unless the kube-apiserver keeps re-generating DEK seeds in pathological cases), so far most of the clusters we have seen have lower than 50 DEK seeds in the cache even though the cluster has been running for many years. 
Hence, we can consider replace the current expiring cache implementation with **non-expiring LRU cache** (e.g. with 1024 size) so that we don't need to rotate the cache on a day basis --- this helps improving the cluster's resilience to KMS service failures, say the KMS service is down for 5 minutes and if the cluster happens to rotate the cache during the time, it will result in unavailability drop unnecessarily.
Additionally, we can also consider pruning all the occurrences of `useSeed` checks from KMSv2 provider as it's no longer used.

**What happened:**
When modifying only metadata (labels or annotations) in a StatefulSet's pod template spec, the StatefulSet controller unnecessarily recreates all pods, causing service disruption for workloads that are otherwise healthy and functioning correctly.
**What you expected to happen:**
Changes to pod metadata (labels/annotations) in the StatefulSet template should be applied directly to existing pods without recreation, similar to how kubectl can directly modify pod labels/annotations without restart.
 
1. Create a StatefulSet with 3 replicas:
 [code] 
2. Wait for all pods to be Running
3. Update only the metadata in the template:
 [code] 
4. This triggers the StatefulSet controller to recreate pods one by one due to template hash change
**Anything else we need to know?:**
This is the documented behavior of StatefulSets where any template change triggers a rolling update based on template hash comparison. However, this creates operational challenges:
- Production workloads suffer unnecessary downtime when adding operational labels (monitoring, alerting, compliance tags)
- The same metadata changes can be applied directly to pods using `kubectl label` or `kubectl annotate` without restart

* if there is at any point no running replica during an upgrade, the upgrade is considered failed
* if there is at any point no quorum during an upgrade, the upgrade is considered failed

title: Prevent Pod Rescheduling When Other Replica is Healthy
body:
### What would you like to be added?
#### Problem Statement
Currently, when a node fails, Kubernetes reschedules pods onto other nodes even if another healthy replica exists on a different node. This behavior can lead to unnecessary resource usage, overloading of remaining nodes, and increased costs in environments where resource optimization is critical.
#### Proposed Solution
Introduce a new field in the Deployment or Pod spec, such as `preventRescheduleIfHealthy: true` or `maxUnavailable: 1`. When this field is set, the Kubernetes scheduler would check if another healthy replica of the same application is running on a different node. If a healthy replica exists, the scheduler would skip rescheduling the failed pod until the healthy replica becomes unhealthy or the node is restored.
#### Alternatives Considered
I explored using Pod Anti-Affinity to ensure replicas are not co-located on the same node, but this does not prevent rescheduling when a node fails. I also considered writing a custom controller to enforce this behavior, but this approach is complex, error-prone, and not scalable. A native Kubernetes feature would provide a more robust and maintainable solution.

title: Add configuration property to delete cronjobs if it succeeds after retry
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Add a boolean cronjob property `deleteFailedJobsOnSuccess` that, when set to `true`, will effectively delete the failed jobs history of that cronjob when it succeeds based on retries dependent on `backoffLimit`.

So e.g. `backoffLimit: 2` and the 1. run fails, but the 2. succeeds, the 1. failed job should not be kept in history.

### Why is this needed?

Sometimes cronjob fail because of temporary issues e.g. database not reachable for short amount of time, then the cronjob succeeds when it automatically runs again, but the failed job is still in the job history.

Setting `failedJobsHistoryLimit: 0` is not a solution as jobs are also not kept when the cronjob fails all the time.

Setting `ttlSecondsAfterFinished` (if possible for cronjobs) is also not a solution as the time is highly dependent on the schedule and has to be calculated to keep a failed job for some time until the next schedule, also the kept failed job might still be unnecessary as the cronjob could have been successful after a direct retry.

title: New EvictionBlocked PodDisruptionCondition
body:
### What would you like to be added?

A EvictionByEvictionAPI [pod disruption condition](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/disruptions/#pod-disruption-conditions) already exists. Suggesting a EvictionBlocked condition be added to know when a eviction is being attempted but blocked by a pod disruption budget at api server


### Why is this needed?

Controllers (autoscalers, customer operators and replicaset/statefulset) have no insight into failed evictions. So if a pod disruption budget is at allowedDisruptions == 0 either because some pods are having errors or becasue the pdb is just very "tight" by default (minAvailable == replicacount), then the controller can't preemptively take action and scale out of the problem. 

Workarounds today include a webhook on evictions but that seems a bit unnatural as you're not validating or mutating the evictions you're essentially watching them. If we use a Pod Disruption Condition instead then controllers can just watch pods which many are already doing. 

Here's an example of a trivial project that would benefit from this [paulgmiller/k8s-pdb-autoscaler](https://github.com/paulgmiller/k8s-pdb-autoscaler) but the hope is this would be beneficial to lots of controllers

title: kubectl explain: add an -o skeleton output format for a copy-pasteable YAML starting point
body:
cc @kubernetes/sig-cli-feature-requests
## What would you like to be added?
A new `kubectl explain <type> -o skeleton` output format that renders a
resource's schema as a concise, editable YAML skeleton (field names with
placeholder values) instead of the verbose field-by-field prose that
`plaintext`/`plaintext-openapiv2` produce.
A companion `-o skeleton-comments` renders the same skeleton with short
inline `# ...` comments for fields that need explaining: `# required`,
`# enum: A|B|C`, `# map[string]string`, and a drill-down hint for fields
collapsed for depth (see below).
Example, `kubectl explain deployments.spec.template.spec.containers -o skeleton`:
 [code] 
Design notes:
- Placeholder values come from the schema's own `default`, else the first
 `enum` value, else `example`, else a type-appropriate zero value. A
 required field with none of those (typically a bare string) gets the
 literal `"<required>"` sentinel so it isn't mistaken for an intentionally
 empty optional field.
- The `status` subresource and server-managed `metadata` fields
 (`resourceVersion`, `uid`, `managedFields`, etc.) are omitted, since nobody
 hand-authors those.

title: kubectl: accept "get logs" as alias to "logs"

## Background
Users often type "kubectl get ...", so it is natural to try "kubectl get logs". Today that fails or behaves differently than "kubectl logs", which is a small UX papercut for both new and experienced users.
## Proposed behavior
Accept "kubectl get logs" and route it to "kubectl logs", matching flags, behavior, and output.
## Examples
- kubectl logs POD
- kubectl get logs POD
- kubectl get logs POD -c CONTAINER
- kubectl get logs -f POD
## Backwards compatibility
This only adds a new accepted invocation and does not change existing command behavior.
## Questions for maintainers
- Would you prefer a simple alias, a "get" subcommand hook, or command routing in kubectl?
- Does this align with current kubectl UX guidelines?

title: Kubectl apply does not remove manually added env vars, causing permanent drift between manifest and live Deployment
body:
### What would you like to be added?
What happened?
We manage Deployments declaratively using kubectl apply (server-side apply) from GitOps pipelines.
In production, a user manually edited a Deployment (kubectl edit deployment) and added an extra environment variable directly under:
spec.template.spec.containers[].env
Later, the Deployment was redeployed using kubectl apply -f <manifest.yaml> with a manifest that does not contain this manually added env var.
Despite successful apply and no reported conflicts, the manually added environment variable remains present in the live Deployment.
This results in permanent configuration drift between the manifest and the cluster state.
### Why is this needed?
We expected the live Deployment to exactly match the applied manifest, such that:
Environment variables not present in the manifest are removed from the Deployment
kubectl apply enforces declarative state, even for mergeable lists like env
The applied manifest becomes the source of truth
In short:
After apply, the cluster state should be fully in sync with the manifest.
**How can we reproduce it**
1. create a deployment
 apiVersion: apps/v1
 kind: Deployment
 metadata:
 name: sample-app
 spec:
 replicas: 1
 selector:
 matchLabels:
 app: sample
 template:
 metadata:
 labels:
 app: sample
 spec:
 containers:
 - name: app
 image: nginx
 env:
 - name: Testing
 value: "working"
 
 kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
2. Manually edit the Deployment
 kubectl edit deployment sample-app
 
 en

title: Update vendored hnslib to v0.1.2 in Kubernetes
body:
**Description**
Kubernetes currently vendors an older version of hnslib for Windows networking / kube-proxy functionality. We would like to update the vendored version to hnslib v0.1.2.
This update brings important improvements for Windows kube-proxy and HNS interactions and aligns Kubernetes with the latest upstream hnslib.
**Motivation / Problem Statement**
Windows kube-proxy relies on hnslib (via hcsshim) for programming HNS networks, load balancers, and policies.
The currently vendored version is missing several fixes and enhancements that are available in hnslib v0.1.2, resulting in limited functionality and additional maintenance burden in Kubernetes.
**Major Updates in hnslib v0.1.2**
The following are the key changes introduced in hnslib v0.1.2 that motivate this update:
- **Dropped archived dependency**: Removed the deprecated and archived dependency: `github.com/pkg/errors` in favor of standard Go error handling.
- **Updated to latest HNS version:** hnslib is updated to work with the latest HNS APIs, including support for ModifyLoadBalancerPolicy, which allows updating existing load balancer policies instead of delete-and-recreate flows.
- **Added flags field to Network Subnets**: Introduced a flags field for network subnets, enabling additional configurability and better parity with evolving HNS capabilities.
These updates improve stability, correctness, and extensibility of Windows networking in Kubernetes.

### What happened?
## Summary
We are experiencing frequent `OOMKilled` failures in our GitLab Runner Kubernetes executor when running Java-based build jobs for one of our customers. The affected jobs allocate memory quickly but remain *within* the configured memory limits. Kubernetes appears to terminate the `build` container prematurely due to the *rate* of memory allocation rather than actual memory pressure.
This leads to multiple failed pipeline runs per day and requires manual restarts or adjustments.
---
## Runner / Environment Details
- **GitLab Runner version:** 18.5.0 (`bda84871`)
- **Executor:** Kubernetes
- **Namespace:** `gitlab-runner`

- **Image:** customer-provided build container

Error in container build: exit code: 137, reason: 'OOMKilled'
---

The build pod stays in **Pending** for an extended period due to:
ContainersNotReady: "containers with unready status: [build helper]"
arduino
Code kopieren
Once the job starts, the Java process fails:
ERROR: Job failed (system failure): Error in container build: exit code: 137, reason: 'OOMKilled'
This occurs **multiple times per day** for our customer.
---
## What We Suspect
Potential contributing factors include:
- Kubernetes memory throttling or prediction mechanisms 
- Container runtime conservative memory heuristics 
- Java `AlwaysPreTouch` rapidly touching memory pages

title: [sig-node] Investigating Unexpected Memory Usage in Kubernetes Pods Causing Restarts
body:
I’m encountering an issue with memory management in my Kubernetes setup, where specific pods are consuming unexpected amounts of memory, leading to frequent restarts. I’d appreciate any guidance on diagnosing this issue and understanding what might be causing the memory consumption.

**Problem Description**

In our current Kubernetes setup, certain pods are writing heavily to memory, eventually consuming the allotted memory limits, which causes them to be terminated and restarted by the system. This behavior disrupts the workload, and we are unclear on what specifically is writing to memory or why this memory consumption is happening.

Since my end goal is to store this data on a Persistent Volume (PVC) instead, if we can identify the process causing this memory usage, I could redirect it to disk storage and avoid filling up memory.

Here’s what I have attempted to understand and troubleshoot this issue:

**Using kubectl describe and kubectl top:**
- Used kubectl describe pod to check for any signs of memory leaks or OOMKill events. Executed kubectl top pod to monitor current memory consumption and identify spikes.

**Setting Resource Limits:**
- Defined resource limits in the pod’s YAML file to ensure it doesn’t exceed a set amount of memory. However, the pod still eventually reaches this limit, indicating continuous high memory use.

**In-pod Process Analysis:**
- Accessed the pod with kubectl exec and ran top -o %MEM to identify any memory-heavy processes.

title: when upgrading kubelet, static pods are always killled even no manifest files are changed
body:
### What happened?
we are upgrading kubelet from 1.16 to 1.18, and find that all those static pods are recreated during the upgrading process.

This is because the static pod hash is a calculation of the `pod *api.Pod`, and the pod spec struct is updated when upgrading to 1.18: `PodSecurityContext.FSGroupChangePolicy` is added.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/config/common.go#L59

So kubelet could not find the container by the new pod hash, even no manifest files are changed.

We notice that those non static pods are not restart, as it has been fixed by this PR #57741
Is it possible to calculate the pod hash by the marshal string of pod struct, to avoid this unnecessary restart?
### What did you expect to happen?
If no manifest files are changed, static pods should not be killed when upgrading kubelet.
### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?
on a kubernetes 1.16 version

title: When publishNotReadyAddresses is set to true, Services route traffic to not-ready Pods anyway
body:
### What happened?

When creating a set of pods behind a service facade (with **_publishNotReadyAddresses=true_**), from which only one pod is marked as ready (albeit they're all running), traffic hitting the service IP gets routed to all pods, not just the ready one(s).

It's possible this is a side-effect of hard-wiring the _**ready**_ attribute in _EndpointSlice_ to _**true**_ (as documented [here](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/endpoint-slices/#ready)).

It seems to me that traffic should only be routed to the pods if _**both**_ _ready_ and _serving_ are _**true**_. The observed behavior contradicts the [documentation of the publishNotReadyAddresses flag](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/dns-pod-service/).

title: Allow both TCP and UDP ports in the same service of type `LoadBalancer`
body:
#### What would you like to be added:
Currently, it is not possible to support both TCP and UDP services with the same service when it is of type `LoadBalancer`. For instance the following spec fails
 [code] 
with the following error message (in v1.21)
> The Service "nginx-https" is invalid: spec.ports: Invalid value: []core.ServicePort{core.ServicePort{Name:"https-tcp", Protocol:"TCP", AppProtocol:(*string)(nil), Port:443, TargetPort:intstr.IntOrString{Type:0, IntVal:8443, StrVal:""}, NodePort:0}, core.ServicePort{Name:"https-quic", Protocol:"UDP", AppProtocol:(*string)(nil), Port:443, TargetPort:intstr.IntOrString{Type:0, IntVal:8443, StrVal:""}, NodePort:0}}: may not contain more than 1 protocol when type is 'LoadBalancer'

#### Why is this needed:
This is needed to support **both HTTP/2 over TLS+TCP and HTTP/3 over QUIC on the same port (here, 443)** so that clients can use either of them without having to know the port for both of them or not having different IP for TCP+TLS and QUIC. It also allows clients to switch if they support (think Google Chrome). I checked that it is possible at pod level to specify the same port, but with different protocols

title: The traffic is not routed correctly after the network interface on worker node is restarted
body:
#### What happened:
We have a statefulset with 2 replicas, on each pod there is Postgres instance. One acts as master while the other acts as replica.
There are 2 services exposed, one is PG master service and the other is PG replica service. Both services are without selector, and there are 2 endpoints sharing the name of it related service.
The IP of the Postgres pod will be patched into endpoints so that the traffic can be routed to the correct pod when accessing the service.
For example, PG master service is corresponding to the endpoint of the same name, and in that endpoint there is ip of the pod running master Postgres instance.

There is another traffic pod which will set up the DB connection to the master Postgres service.
The problem is:
1. The traffic pod(issue DB connections with JDBC) and PG master pod are in the same worker node(let’s call it worker1).
2. The PG replica pod is in another worker(worker2).
3. Run a testing case which is: “Shutdown network interface on worker1, sleep 60s, take up network interface on worker1”
4. Then the previous PG replica pod is promoted to master, and the previous PG master pod is demoted to replica.
5. The traffic pod’s target address is the PG master service name but at that time it connects to the replica pod. Thus the traffic could try to write to a PG in ‘read-only’ mode and test case fails.

The kube-proxy mode is iptables.
We suspect the iptables in kube-proxy doesn’t update the routing information in time.

title: [workqueue] Monitor the full latency of items added to the rate-limit queue
body:
When an item is added to a rate-limiting queue, users may want visibility into how long a key has been waiting before it's actually added to the queue (i.e., the delay duration). This can be helpful to understand the extent of rate limiting in a controller’s traffic patterns.
I believe it would be useful to expose one more metric in [waitForPriorityQueue](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/master/util/workqueue/delaying_queue.go#L199), similar to how the [latency](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/master/util/workqueue/metrics.go#L112) of the queue is measured. 
Another option is to have users wrap the queue and track timestamps in the application code. Given that we already track the [retry](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/master/util/workqueue/delaying_queue.go#L154) count, it seems cleaner to me to add a new metric to the library directly. 
Happy to contribute a patch if the team agrees this would be a worthwhile addition.
Thanks!

title: Does anyone know why version 28 of apiserver uses two versions of openAPI? Two openAPI.installs are called in preparerun, one is v3 and the other is v2
Leader election acquire loop should fail if the cluster is not reachable.
body:
### Problem:
The leader election acquisition loops currently attempts indefinitely to acquire a leader, even if the cluster is unreachable. 
### Proposed Solution:
We should introduce a configurable timeout to bail out and fail the leader election process if the cluster is not reachable within a specified time. By default, we can retain the current behavior of indefinite retries, but we should allow users to configure this timeout, either to enable the timeout or to adjust its duration.

title: client library module versioning
body:
> I am well aware of the storied past that kubernetes has had with module versioning, thus I will try and work off the [current state](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go#versioning) of the world, but it would be interesting to understand how this impacts old projects virally entangled with [replace](https://go.dev/doc/modules/gomod-ref#replace).

If I am developing an internal tool that only imports `k8s.io/client-go/...` and only runs on a cluster that I control, I can trivially pick the exact kubernetes version that I am running, `go get k8s.io/client-go@v0.X.Y` and be happy.

Per [KEP 917](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-architecture/917-go-modules), "consumers are limited to a single copy of kubernetes libraries among all dependencies". As such, if I am running two clusters with different versions and I actually need `v0.20.0` and `v0.21.0`, say due to a feature deprecation, I need to maintain two different versions of my tool?

Taking this a step further, if I maintain a tool that contains a library component and links against the `k8s.io/...` packages, do I need to release separate versions for every kubernetes minor?

Finally, I apologize if this is covered in a document or manual somewhere, but I cannot find it documented anywhere; hence my creation of this issue.

title: Optimize the memory usage.
body:
**What would you like to be added**:
- Pod managed by deployment can be stored in memory in a more memory friendly way. As all the pod specs are almost the same(except for the `Nodename` field?). We can share one copy in the memory, instead of thousands of it. And we can even store less information in etcd by the same way.
- Optimize the serialization. Most of the memory are consumed by serializations triggered by all kinds of requests. The client fetches all the information about the object from apiserver, but in most situations, the client only needs a few field about the object, and the apiserver has to serialize the whole object, which is both cpu-intensive and memory-intensive. Can we provide a more flexible API to provide only the information the client needs?

**Why is this needed**:
We have an 2000-node-cluster in our production environment. The apiserver consumes too much memory. As the cluster grows much bigger, the situation can be much worse. We already scaled the apiserver number to 6, each was deloyed on a physical machine of 200GB memory. We want to find some way to optimize the memory usage instead of adding more machines.

Our [operator ](https://github.com/cloudfoundry-incubator/service-fabrik-broker/tree/master/helm-charts/interoperator) was using a crd.v1beta1.apiextensions.k8s.io and recently updated to crd.v1.apiextensions.k8s.io. In v1beta1 definition `spec.preserveUnknownFields` set as true. In the v1 version some fields have the `x-kubernetes-preserve-unknown-fields` set as true. Our operator copies the crds to another cluster and this fails with
 [code]

 [code] 

Created a Validating Webhook pointing to port 8000:

 [code]

After fixing the webhook configuration, I started seeing the message:
 [code] 

Consistently when hitting one of the masters, while the Validating Webhook worked as expected when hitting the other master. Again the weird character 'ƻ' represents 443, the .webhooks[].clientConfig.service.port in ValidatingWebhookConfiguration.

The same issue persists after deleting the service, webhook, and recreating with the same names.

 :
I expected the Validating Webhook to work on both masters.

 :
Tried reproducing this issue using a different service name, as well as deploying it in another cluster. But the same error didn't happen again, so I believe there was some sort of special condition that caused this problem.

 :
Digging a bit into this, I suspect it has something to do with the [caching](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.15/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/webhook/client.go#L117) . I couldn't find a reference to where this cache is cleaned up.

title: Topology Spread Constraints does not respect taints
body:
### What happened?
Created a kind cluster with one control plane node and three worker nodes. Created a deployment with 7 replicas and topology constraint with key `kubernetes.io/hostname` and `maxSkew` set to 1. Only three pods got scheduled; others are in pending state.
### What did you expect to happen?
All seven pods get scheduled in three worker nodes with a distribution of (2,2,3). 

The filter takes the control plane node into account. The control plane node has a taint and no pods (except the one having toleration) can be scheduled there. For three pods, the distribution is (0,1,1,1) where the first element represents the control plane node. Scheduling any more pods is not possible; adding to control plane node is not possible because of the taint; adding to any of the worker nodes is not possible as it will violate the topology spread constraints.

It's understandable that the plugin works as expected. But, it's good to incorporate the intelligence of ignoring the tainted nodes.

title: Default storage class needs to be present before PVCs are created
body:
#### What happened:

When the PVC is created before the default storage class, PVC will end up in a state with no storage class and will never be bounded to a PV.

#### What you expected to happen:

I expect that in eventually consistent model of Kubernetes, non-bound PVCs with no storage class will get assigned the default class once one is available and get bounded to a PV.

#### How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):

Create a PVC with no storage class, and then create a StorageClass marked as default.

#### Anything else we need to know?:

The setter of the default storage class on PVCs is currently implemented only as an admission webhook, creating the requirements for the default StorageClass to exist before any PVCs are created. I think similar logic should be executed in PV controller to add the default storage class if PVC is not bound and doesn't have a storage class.

#### Environment:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): 1.19.4

title: Is it possible for a PV to be mounted on the same node twice
body:
I am recently working on the CSI plugin... when using PV/PVC with deployment some interesting things occurred.

although the PV/PVC was set as `ReadWriteOnce`, it's possible 2 pods from different replicas that use the same pvc. if both the pods was scheduled to 1 node, the so called `isMultiAttachForbidden` in controller manager cannot detect any issue, instead both pod will be running on the same node sharing same PV(and its underlying remote disk)

In above case, the first detach(remove the pod) should not remove access of the node to the disk, while detach(by calling CSI grpc) happens on the controller side, it's not easy to detect this dilemma whether to remove access of the node..


Any suggestion or comments is welcome

title: Creating the pod requested bidirectional propagation will succeed even when kubelet/kubeapi 's `MountPropagation = false`
body:
**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**:

 


 :
Create a pod with `MountPropagation: bidirectional` in a cluster with both kube-apiserver and kubelet have `MountPropagation = false`. The creation will succeed. And the `mountPropagation` option for the volume would be removed silently from the pod's spec.

 :
The pod creation should fail in some way since the requirement cannot be satisfied.

Otherwise, the caller cannot know if the result is expected or not.

 :
1. Create a cluster with `MountPropagation = false` for both kubelet and kube-apiserver
2. Create a pod requested `MountPropagation: bidirectional`
3. The pod was created successfully. The `mountPropagation` option for the volume has been removed silently from the pod's spec.

 :

title: KeyUsage array content changed in 1.27 for a non-RSA key
body:
### What happened?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/111660

This PR changed the KeyUsage array from including 3 items to 2 in non RSA key case. KeyUsage is defined https://github.com/kubernetes/api/blob/master/certificates/v1/types.go#L124.

Hence starting 1.27 the [CertificateSigningRequest](https://github.com/kubernetes/api/blob/master/certificates/v1/types.go#L41) content actually changed but the version doesn't change accordingly.

This breaks a scenario in EKS with fargate where a non-RSA key is used. For example `kubectl exec` fails.

### What did you expect to happen?

title: Increase log level for TLS handshake error logs for kube-apiserver
body:
:

Then load balancer probes kube-apiserver in TCP mode, every probe logs `http: TLS handshake error from ...` message in `kube-apiserver` logs on default log level and this is annoying, it bloats the logs all over and makes debugging more difficult.

 :

kube-apiserver should log those errors only on highre log levels (even 2 will be an improvement).

 :

1. Start kube-apiserver
2. Do `telnet <apiserver address>`

 :

As a follow up to prematurely closed #70411, and as suggested in the comments there (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/70411#issuecomment-616094579), I suggest we increase the log level for those log messages so they don't get printed by default.

title: Is there a way to filter and process login request to kube-api-server?
body:
Our goal is to deny login using token from service accounts. 

What we plan is to

1. Capture login event 
2. Forward request to an OPA instance
3. OPA will check if the login request is using a token. It will deny user from logging in if it's using a token, otherwise it will allow it. 
4. Allowed request will be forwarded to the auth server/ identity provider so that it will not be touched and business for him as usual

@kubernetes/sig-auth

title: pod name and host name differ in indexed completion mode
body:
In case[ .spec.completionMode = Indexed](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/job/#completion-mode) in our Kubernetes job yaml,
The host name will look like (in /etc/hostname in a pod container) looks like:
'xxxxxxxxx-0'
'xxxxxxxxx-1'
'xxxxxxxxx-2'
etc.
However,
The pod name will be:
'xxxxxxxxx-0-{randomid}'
'xxxxxxxxx-1-{randomid}'
'xxxxxxxxx-2-{randomid}'
etc.
Why is the pod name not set identical to the host name? 
In case of .spec.completionMode=NonIndexed mode pod name and hostname are identical. 
So this is an unexpected inconsistency.
The random id can be left out: xxxxxxxxx-{IndexNr} is already an unique id.
It is important, because we let our containers write their hostname in our log messages.
However, we cannot directly derive the pod name from the host name, which is needed to find back the pod logs written to persistent storage later on.
Of course we can work around this, by adding the pod name to the env variables of the container and log that additionally, but that should not be necessary in my opinion. It is very confusing that pod name and host name differ in indexed mode.

title: How about supports ETL job scheduler?

We have many ETL jobs and preparing transfer these jobs running on k8s. Here is my demands and ideas:

1. Jobs on k8s should have dependency relation.
2. Support CRON syntax, [CronJob](http://kubernetes.io/docs/user-guide/cron-jobs/) can do this.

body:
**Client Version**: v1.13.1
**Server Version**: v1.17.9

**Background**:
We were updating config maps using `kubectl apply -f configmap.yaml`. At a point, we started facing issue with `apply` as the size of the metadata was more than the limit. As we understand it, the metadata field keeps previous version of configmap. It's weird to understand why configmap itself doesn't have limit, but metadata field does(We would like to know the reason)
When started facing this issue, we found that `kubectl replace` command doesn't maintain this metadata and we could use it in our case.
As a deployment process, we first `replace` the config map. After its successful, we then `apply` the deployments.yaml.

**Expected Behaviour**:
When we replace configmap and restart our pods, changes must be available in all pods.

**Actual Behaviour**:
With `kubectl replace` command, we observed that, post deployment few pods are seen w/ changes in configmap but few don't have the changes and it's happening randomly.

Could someone please help us understand this? Is it a bug or we are doing something incorrectly?

title: Password in secret being wrongly decoded
body:
Hi!
I was setting up a kubernetes cluster today and the pod wasn't able to pull the image from docker complaining about invalid credentials. I use a password manager with all the options on, so it uses everything possible to create a password.

I followed the instructions of creating a secret using kubectl and the secret is created successfully, but when I decoded it to verify its contents after googling everywhere and not finding any solution, I found that the password was different from the one I inputted.
Essentially, the password contained an "&" char, and when it is decoded, instead of it being an "&" char, it was \u0026, so the password broke.

Doing a base64 encode/decode of the "&" powershell works correctly, so I'm assuming that there is some problem on kubernetes side.
